prose.def: To press or urge a point with greater force or urgency, often with fierce or aggressive insistence.
prose.article: This verb combines "upon" (ἐπί) with "to be strong" (ἰσχύω), giving the picture of someone strengthening or intensifying their effort — in practice, pressing a point more urgently. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 23:5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "insisting" (matched 100% by the Berean Standard Bible). The everyday flavor is confirmed by Koine papyri, and a striking parallel from Vettius Valens uses it of an argument that "will be stronger" for advice or instruction; in the Septuagint (Sirach 29:1, 1 Maccabees 6:6) it can simply mean to make or grow stronger.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and an overall low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin.

prose.def: To heap up or accumulate for oneself, used figuratively in the NT of self-servingly amassing teachers to suit one's own desires.
prose.article: This verb means to pile something up in growing quantity, combining the idea of 'heaping' with the prefix meaning 'upon' or 'in addition.' It appears just once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 4:3), where it describes people gathering teachers for themselves; the corpus shows it absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. Everyday Koine papyri attest the same sense, and Epictetus uses it of someone who 'has gone on adding to his heap ever since' — a vivid picture of relentless accumulation.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on thin evidence.

prose.def: An authoritative command or order, used especially of God's binding commission to Paul and of human directives issued with recognized authority.
prose.article: ἐπιταγή means a command or order given by someone with the authority to issue it, appearing 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The renderings cluster tightly around "command" (5×, or 71%), with the remaining occurrences in Titus describing a command delivered with full authority. Notably, dedicatory inscriptions used the phrase κατ᾽ ἐπιταγήν to mean "by divine command" — an altar set up because a god ordered it in a dream or oracle — which matches Paul's use of the word for God's commands.
prose.caution: The two single-occurrence senses in Titus reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings, and the underlying sense is consistently "command."

prose.def: To issue an authoritative command or directive to someone, used actively or passively across a range of syntactic constructions (dative of person, accusative of thing, infinitive).
prose.article: ἐπιτάσσω means to command or give an authoritative order, built from ἐπί ("upon") and τάσσω ("arrange"), so literally something like "arrange upon" — to lay a directive on someone. It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often with the person commanded in the dative and the thing commanded as an object or infinitive. The everyday papyri show this same plain force: one Oxyrhynchus letter from A.D. 32 has a worker reassuring his employer, "I did not neglect your instructions," showing the word used for ordinary commands given and obeyed.
prose.caution: The Septuagint Hebrew counterparts in the digest (חָתַם "seal," אַף "anger/nostril," גָּוַע "expire") don't obviously match "command," so the LXX evidence here is murky and may reflect alignment noise rather than real sense range.

prose.def: To bring a task, duty, or ritual fully to completion; in the middle voice, to complete something for oneself or to perform (religious rites).
senseLabels: to perform religious or cultic duties
prose.article: ἐπιτελέω means to bring something all the way to completion—to finish, accomplish, or fully carry out a task. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times across 7 books, and the Majority Standard Bible most clearly renders it "completed," though in 5 of those 11 cases its meaning is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. A nice detail from the everyday papyri is that the verb often describes performing religious duties—one document speaks of "performing the services of the gods"—which lines up with its New Testament use in Hebrews for carrying out priestly rituals.
prose.caution: The classical lexicons note a middle-voice sense ("make an end of oneself" in Galatians 3:3, or "pay in full" in 1 Peter 5:9) that the measured data does not separately track, so its full range is broader than the single rendering shown.

prose.def: Fitting or necessary for a purpose; in its NT plural form (τὰ ἐπιτήδεια), the basic necessities or provisions a person needs.
senseLabels: necessities / basic provisions (plural substantive τὰ ἐπιτήδεια)
prose.article: This adjective describes what is fitting, useful, or necessary, and in its plural form (τὰ ἐπιτήδεια) it means "the necessities of life." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in James 2:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the "physical" things a needy person requires. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: documents speak of making payments "for necessaries" and furnishing provisions and supplies, even for huntsmen, showing the word was common business language for basic goods.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint match, the measured evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

prose.def: To place, lay, or impose something on a person or thing, whether in healing or blessing, physical burden, hostile act, or formal addition.
prose.article: At its core ἐπιτίθημι means to set or lay one thing upon another, built from ἐπί ("on") and τίθημι ("put"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 41 times, rendered "place" in 12 (55%) and "laid" in 8 (36%), though in 19 of those it dissolves into the surrounding English phrasing with no word of its own. A frequent special use is the laying on of hands — for blessing, healing, or commissioning, as when Jesus places his hands on the blind or sick. Strong's notes it can carry either a friendly or hostile sense ("impose"), and the Septuagint uses it heavily, 239 times across 26 books, often for the Hebrew śûm ("set," 28×) and sāmak ("lean, lay on," 24×).

prose.def: To rebuke, admonish, or sternly warn someone, sometimes with a command to stop; used of Jesus, disciples, and in pastoral or cosmic contexts.
prose.article: This verb means to speak sharply to someone — rebuking, scolding, or firmly warning them, frequently with a command to stop or be quiet. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 29 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "rebuked" or "Jesus rebuked" in 75% of cases, with a smaller group (7%) carrying the sense of a stern warning. In everyday Koine papyri the word could even mean to lay someone under a penalty or fine, and in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew גָּעַר ("to rebuke"), as in Zechariah 3:2.

prose.def: A punishment or penalty imposed as discipline on someone who has done wrong.
prose.article: In the New Testament this word appears just once (2 Corinthians 2:6), where it refers to a punishment or penalty the community has imposed on an offender. Interestingly, the word originally meant something quite different — "citizenship" or "franchise" — and that older sense still turns up in a third-century rescript of Severus among the papyri. The penalty meaning, by contrast, is paralleled in everyday legal documents (for example, papyri threatening triple penalties) and matches the related word ἐπιτίμιον, plus its one appearance in the Septuagint at Wisdom 3:10.
prose.caution: This is a hapax in the New Testament with only one Septuagint parallel, and lexicons split it between two very different senses (citizenship versus penalty), so confidence in its precise range is low.

prose.def: To permit or allow someone to do something, sometimes in a passive sense of permission being received or subject to divine will.
prose.article: ἐπιτρέπω is the standard Koine word for letting someone do something or granting permission, appearing 19 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "permitted" 8 times, "let" 4 times, and "permission" 3 times — all clustering tightly around the single idea of allowing. The everyday papyri confirm this exact sense: one petition from 221 B.C. begs a king "not to permit" an opponent to obstruct building work, showing the word at home in ordinary requests and legal pleas. The older lexica add an underlying notion of "turn over, commit, entrust," but the measured New Testament usage is consistently about permission.

prose.article: ἐπιτροπή refers to delegated authority — the official power or commission to act, decide, or carry something out on behalf of someone else. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "pursuit" while the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) favor "power to decide, authority" and the KJV reads "commission." The everyday papyri are especially telling here: in one document a person says they handed over the ἐπιτροπή "to the gods," and the word commonly means the office of a legal guardian, as in receipts demanding proof of guardianship.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use — and the measured rendering "pursuit" diverges from the lexicons, which point to "authority" or "commission."

prose.def: A person put in charge of someone else's affairs—either a household manager or a legal guardian appointed over minors.
prose.article: ἐπίτροπος is someone entrusted with another's responsibilities, ranging from a household steward or estate manager (Matthew 20:8, Luke 8:3) to a legal guardian set over children (Galatians 4:2). All 3 of its New Testament occurrences are folded into surrounding phrasing rather than mapped to a single English word. The everyday papyri make the legal sense vivid: one document records 'Aurelius Hermodorus, guardian of the minors,' taking an oath on their behalf, and wills routinely name ἐπίτροποι to oversee heirs until they came of age.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences across 3 books, all absorbed into phrasing, so the sense divisions rest mainly on context and outside sources.

prose.def: To attain or successfully reach a goal or desired object; rendered negatively when its clause contains a negation (e.g., 'did not obtain').
prose.article: ἐπιτυγχάνω means to attain or hit the mark — to successfully reach the thing you are after, whether a promise (Hebrews 6:15) or what you crave (James 4:2). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders each occurrence slightly differently depending on context, even using it negatively in Romans 11:7 where Israel "failed to obtain" what it sought. One nice detail: the lexicographer Hort argued the word doesn't strictly mean "get possession" but rather "attain" or "be successful," and a 2nd-century papyrus backs this up, where someone writes that through friends' help "we achieved it."
prose.caution: The classical lexica note the word can take either the genitive (older usage) or accusative (later Greek), and Hort disputes the common gloss "obtain," so its exact force is debated.

prose.def: To shine upon or appear visibly, used of light guiding people and of God's grace or kindness making itself known.
senseLabels: to shine upon, giving light and guidance

prose.article: At its core ἐπιφαίνω means to shine upon and so become visible or known, built from ἐπί ("upon") and φαίνω ("shine"). In the New Testament it appears just 4 times, half rendered "appeared," while individual cases describe light shining to guide a path (Luke 1:79) and God's saving grace appearing (Titus 2:11). The most striking evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions: the same word was used for the "epiphany" of the goddess Artemis appearing to worshippers, the very language Moulton-Milligan links to its use in Titus.
prose.caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the three rendered "senses" overlap heavily and largely reflect context rather than distinct meanings.

prose.article: ἐπιφάνεια means an "appearing" or "manifestation"—a moment when someone or something becomes visibly present. prose.caution: The measured sense breakdown contains several garbled labels ("charge view His," "now His appearing") that appear to be data artifacts; the genuine consistent meaning is simply "appearing/appearance."

prose.def: To shine upon something or someone; used as an imperative call for Christ's light to illuminate, with directional force implied by the ἐπι- prefix.

prose.article: This rare verb means to shine upon or give light, and in its single New Testament appearance (Ephesians 5:14) it is used figuratively, as in the call for Christ to shine on the one who awakes. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, with the Septuagint using it just three times, all in Job. Notably, in Job it renders three different Hebrew words, including one tied to the brightness of the moon (Job 31:26), showing its core sense of light shining forth.
prose.caution: This word is barely attested — one Byzantine occurrence (none in the critical text) and only three in the Septuagint — and lexicons note textual variants and confusion with related forms, so confidence is low.

issues: The syntactic role data shows the single NT occurrence is vocative, meaning the verb appears as an imperative address ('shine upon!'), not a straightforward indicative or infinitive use — the definition does not reflect this imperative/command nuance
The sense label '1. O' is a placeholder or encoding artifact, not a meaningful semantic label

The supporting article states the LXX uses the word in Job for three Hebrew words including יָרֵ֫חַ (moon) and עֲטִישֹׁת (sneezing/flashing), but the definition omits the 'shine forth' directional nuance (ἐπι- prefix) that Abbott-Smith and Dodson both highlight
The article conflates ἐπιφαύω with ἐπιφαύσκω — Abbott-Smith treats ἐπιφαύσκω as the base form and ἐπιφαύω as a variant, which the definition does not acknowledge

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence, used as an imperative ('shine upon') addressed to the sleeper, confirming the figurative illumination sense but also demonstrating the command/vocative register the definition underplays
The BSB independently renders this as a command for Christ to shine upon the sleeper, supporting the 'shine upon' gloss but showing the directional ἐπι- sense ('upon') is integral to meaning
Abbott-Smith's note on textual variants (ἐπιψαύσει) at this verse confirms the low-confidence caution is warranted and that the lemma identity itself is debated

audit.author_note: The word appears only in Pauline material (Ephesians), so no cross-author comparison is possible; the definition should acknowledge this is a hapax in Pauline usage only.

prose.def: To bring something upon or against someone — especially to inflict a judgment or wrath, or to bring forward a legal charge or accusation.
senseLabels: to bring forward or voice (a charge or claim)
to impose or inflict (wrath or punishment)
to bring a legal charge against
prose.article: At its core ἐπιφέρω combines ἐπί ("upon, against") with φέρω ("carry"), meaning to bring or carry something toward a target — often in a legal or hostile sense like leveling an accusation or imposing a judgment. Across its 5 Byzantine New Testament occurrences each rendering appears just once: "brought," "speak," "highlights," and "charge," so no single sense dominates. The everyday papyri confirm this legal flavor: documents repeatedly use it for producing proofs or certificates in court, as in an Oxyrhynchus text where someone acts "in accordance with the proofs he produced."
prose.caution: With only 5 occurrences spread evenly across four different renderings, the precise sense in any given verse depends heavily on context.

prose.def: To shout or cry out, often repeatedly, in direct address to a person or group — ranging in tone from hostile condemnation to celebratory acclamation.
prose.article: ἐπιφωνέω means to call out or shout at someone, built from ἐπί ("at, toward") and φωνέω ("to make a sound, call"). Across its few New Testament uses it covers crowds shouting condemnation (Luke 23:21), acclaiming a ruler (Acts 12:22), and clamoring a demand (Acts 22:24), so the tone ranges from hostile to celebratory. The everyday Koine papyri match this nicely: one document from A.D. 192 has bystanders shouting "Let Achilles be crowned!", and an inscription records the crowd crying "Well said, Philocles!"
prose.caution: With only 3 Byzantine occurrences (each rendered differently) and thin Septuagint evidence, the precise range is hard to pin down, so this entry sits at low confidence.

prose.def: To begin to grow light or to draw on, marking the onset of a new day — whether sunrise dawn or, in Jewish reckoning, a day beginning at evening.
senseLabels: dawn toward a new day (sunrise context)
draw on, begin (Sabbath/Jewish day at sunset)
prose.article: This verb describes the early light of dawn or the moment a new day begins to draw on. It appears only twice in the New Testament, rendered once with "day" (Matthew 28:1) and once with "beginning" (Luke 23:54), both pointing to the same idea of light breaking. Notably, the everyday papyri show the same usage: a horoscope from A.D. 81 and a later festal letter both use the participle to mark the dawning of a particular day.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin evidence, the exact shade of meaning (literal dawn versus the approach of a day) is not always certain.

prose.def: To undertake or attempt to do something, often implying an effort whose outcome is uncertain or still in progress.
prose.article: ἐπιχειρέω literally means "to put one's hand to" something, and in practice it means to undertake or attempt an action. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Luke's writings, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "tried" or "talked, debated, tried" (Acts 9:29; 19:13), and once it is absorbed into the phrasing. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan cites a 164 B.C. document using it for someone trying "to compel them to accept" the work.
prose.caution: With only 3 NT occurrences and a low confidence tier, the sense range is thinly attested.

prose.def: To pour liquid onto or over something; in the NT, used once of the Good Samaritan pouring oil and wine on wounds (Luke 10:34).
prose.article: This verb simply means to pour something over or onto something — the basic image is liquid spilling onto a surface. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:34, where the Good Samaritan pours oil and wine onto the injured man's wounds. The Septuagint uses it 21 times, most often (16×) for the Hebrew יָצַק, as when Jacob pours oil on the stone at Bethel (Genesis 28:18); everyday Koine papyri also use it concretely, including a warning not to keep pouring when a vessel is already full.
prose.caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured New Testament range rests on a single verse.

prose.def: To supply or furnish something (actively or passively), sometimes with a sense of generosity or abundance, whether God, people, or bodily structures are the source.
prose.article: This compound verb means to supply or provide, frequently with a sense of generosity or abundance — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lavish" in two of five occurrences and "supplies" in another. It appears 5 times across 4 New Testament books, with two more occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. A papyrus complaint from around A.D. 30 captures the generous flavor nicely: a man says he "provided for my wife in a manner that exceeded my resources," showing the everyday Koine sense of giving beyond what is required.

prose.article: ἐπιχορηγία refers to a supply, provision, or support that is furnished to someone or something. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 4:16 and Philippians 1:19), and the standard lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) consistently gloss it as "a supply" or "support." The word was at home in everyday Koine: an inscription (Syll 378.9, A.D. 79-81) speaks of a supply drawn from temple revenues, showing its ordinary use for material provisioning.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences); the second measured sense rendered "distress" reflects translation context rather than the word's own meaning, since the lexica agree it simply means a supply.

prose.def: To make a place or person utterly desolate and ruined, or (of a person) to strip bare; used in the NT almost entirely in apocalyptic and judgment contexts.
prose.article: ἐρημόω means to turn something into a wasteland — to leave a place desolate or to strip a person of everything. It is closely related to ἔρημος, "desert," and the family shows clearly in the Septuagint, where it appears 54 times and most often translates the Hebrew חָרַב, "to be laid waste" (20×). The same word turns up in everyday Koine documents; one papyrus from around A.D. 245 reports that "the lands happened to be laid waste," showing the very physical, practical sense of ruin.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament — only 5 Byzantine occurrences (none in the SBL critical text), and 3 of those are absorbed into phrasing without their own English word.

prose.def: The state of being laid waste or made desolate—a place stripped bare and left in ruins.

In the Septuagint it shows up 18 times and most often translates the Hebrew שִׁקּוּץ (5×), a word for something detestable, alongside terms for being made desolate (שָׁמֵם).
prose.caution: This word appears only 3 times in the New Testament and the confidence tier is low, though all sources agree on its meaning.

prose.def: A self-centered drive to advance personal interests or form rival factions, often at others' expense; can denote party-spirit or rivalry collectively.
prose.article: ἐριθεία describes a self-centered ambition — the drive to advance yourself or gather your own following at others' expense. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "selfish ambition" in 4 of 7 occurrences (80%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 75% of the time; the remaining cases shade toward "self-seeking." Interestingly, the word's roots lie in ordinary working life: Moulton-Milligan trace it to a verb meaning "work for hire," connected to ἔριθος, a wool-weaver attested in Koine papyri, before it developed the sense of scheming for personal advantage.
prose.caution: The word appears only 7 times and 2 of those were absorbed into surrounding phrasing, so its precise range is somewhat thin and the older glosses (KJV's "strife, contention") reflect a different emphasis than the measured "selfish ambition."

prose.def: Wool, the soft fiber shorn from sheep, used in ritual contexts and as a simile for whiteness.
prose.article: ἔριον simply means wool—the fiber from sheep used in textiles. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: at Hebrews 9:19, where scarlet wool was used in a ritual, and at Revelation 1:14, where Christ's hair is described as white as wool. The everyday nature of the word shows up clearly in the papyri, where it turns up in inventories and shipping records measuring out quantities of wool by weight, and the Septuagint uses it 10 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for wool, צֶמֶר.
prose.caution: The first listed "sense" ("proclaimed along wool") simply reflects the surrounding phrase at Hebrews 9:19, not a distinct meaning—both occurrences mean wool.

prose.def: Strife, quarreling, or competitive rivalry among people—hostile discord that fractures community or drives self-serving competition.
prose.article: This word covers the whole range of human conflict, from heated dissension to ongoing quarrels and rivalry, and the three measured senses really differ only in shade rather than substance. It appears 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament, almost always in lists of vices, and the Majority Standard Bible spreads it fairly evenly across "dissension," "quarrels," and "quarrels rivalry." Interestingly, while the New Testament treats it as a clear negative, the everyday Koine evidence is wider: a papyrus love-fragment uses it for "hate" taking hold of someone, yet an inscription uses it in a good sense, of beauty stirring up admiring rivalry in onlookers.
prose.caution: The three measured senses overlap heavily and the MSB's "quarrels" and "rivalry" renderings have 0% independent agreement from BSB, so the boundaries between them are fuzzy.

prose.def: A young goat or kid; in Matthew 25:33 used symbolically by Jesus for those condemned at final judgment, contrasted with sheep representing the righteous.
prose.article: ἐρίφιον is a diminutive of ἔριφος and simply means a young goat or kid. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, where Jesus separates sheep from goats, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a letter (c. B.C. 245) asking that a goat be sent for a coming festival. Some manuscripts read the simpler form ἔριφος in places like Luke 15:29, but the diminutive is well attested in ordinary documents listing livestock.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament: it appears only once, with manuscripts sometimes preferring the related form ἔριφος.

prose.article: ἐρωτάω covers two related actions: asking a question to get information, and asking someone for something — that is, making a request. The questioning sense dominates the Byzantine New Testament, where renderings like "ask" and "asked" account for about 68% of the 58 occurrences, but the requesting sense shows up clearly too (for instance, asking on someone's behalf in Luke 4:38 and John 17:9). In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew שָׁאַל 52 of 64 times, and Moulton-Milligan note it is so well attested in everyday papyri — like a letter urging "I ask you by every means to send me the rest at once" — that there is no need to treat its requesting sense as a Hebrew influence.

prose.article: ἐsthḗs is a general word for clothing or garments, covering everything from a king's splendid robe to ordinary dress. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across 3 books, often pointing to notable or fine attire—a royal robe in Acts 12:21 or the well-dressed visitor in James 2:2. prose.def: To eat or consume food, whether literally at a meal or idiomatically (to live by, to devour); often used in participial constructions meaning 'while eating.'

prose.article: ἐσθίω is the everyday Koine word for eating, and the data bears that out: the Byzantine New Testament uses it 65 times, and translators render it "eat" in 84% of cases, with the rest being "while eating"-type phrases that simply describe the act of dining. Its range is straightforward and literal, though older lexicons note a metaphorical edge—Dodson lists "devour, consume" as rust does, and the KJV occasionally renders it "devour" or "live." In the Septuagint it appears 288 times, almost always translating Hebrew אָכַל ("to eat," 262×), and a charming papyrus letter (P Giss I.80) has a writer asking for "little pigeons and fowl, which I am not accustomed to eat"—proof of how ordinary the word was in daily life.

prose.def: A mirror, in ancient times a polished metal surface used for seeing one's reflection.
prose.article: ἔσοπτρον means a mirror, and in all 2 of its New Testament appearances it is rendered exactly that way. Since ancient mirrors were made of polished metal rather than glass, the reflection they gave was often dim or imperfect — which is the very point Paul draws on in 1 Corinthians 13:12. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a temple property list mentioning a silver mirror made for a child.
prose.caution: With only 2 occurrences the entry rests on thin corpus evidence, though all sources agree on the meaning.

receipts.how: Paul uses ἔσοπτρον explicitly for a mirror whose imperfect reflection illustrates indirect, partial knowledge, confirming the definition's note about polished-metal mirrors giving dim images.

James compares a person who hears the word but does not act to one who looks at his natural face in a mirror (ἔσοπτρον), confirming the word means a reflective surface for seeing one's own appearance.

The KJV gloss 'glass' for ἔσοπτρον might mislead modern readers into thinking of glass mirrors; the definition's clarification that ancient mirrors were polished metal is well-supported here and by Dodson and Moulton-Milligan.

audit.author_note: Paul (1 Corinthians) employs ἔσοπτρον as a theological metaphor for indirect, imperfect knowledge of God, while James uses it in a straightforward behavioral analogy; the word's meaning is identical in both, but the rhetorical weight differs.

prose.def: A year, used to measure durations of time, someone's age (in genitive constructions), or recurring annual events.
prose.article: ἔτος simply means "a year," and it's used very consistently throughout the New Testament. In the Byzantine text it appears 49 times, rendered "years" in 44 cases (94%) and "years old" in just 2 cases when stating someone's age. The everyday papyri confirm this ordinary usage: one document speaks of coming "up to the metropolis at the New Year," and the phrase κατ᾽ ἔτος ("yearly") shows up in a contract requiring annual payments — the same expression found in Luke 2:41. In the Septuagint it occurs 613 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for "year" (שָׁנִים, 550×).

issues: The definition does not account for the 2 occurrences (4%) that are absorbed into phrasing with no own English word rendered, leaving approximately 4% of occurrences unaddressed

The supporting article states the word appears 'very consistently' and implies near-total coverage with just two senses, but the rare rendering 'up for years' and the 2 absorbed occurrences suggest edge cases the definition silently drops

The sense label 'years old' is slightly imprecise; the corpus evidence and Abbott-Smith show this construction uses a genitive of age (ἐτῶν) or εἶναι/γίνεσθαι constructions, meaning the word functions as a genitive noun in an idiomatic age expression rather than a fixed compound gloss

The definition phrase 'basic unit for measuring spans of time or someone's age' conflates two grammatically distinct constructions without signaling that the age sense is an idiomatic genitive construction

receipts.how: A woman who had suffered for twelve years — ἔτη δώδεκα — illustrates the dominant accusative 'years' sense measuring a span of time, confirming the core definition.
'She was twelve years old' uses ἐτῶν δώδεκα, a genitive construction for age, demonstrating the distinct syntactic form behind sense 2 that the definition does not distinguish.
'This temple has been under construction for forty-six years' uses a dative of space of time, one of the absorbed or edge-case constructions the definition does not cover.

audit.author_note: Luke accounts for the largest share of occurrences (15×) and uses ἔτος in both temporal span and age constructions with historical precision (e.g., LUK 3:1 synchronizing regnal years); Revelation uses it distinctively in apocalyptic thousand-year reign passages (6×), giving the word an eschatological register absent from Luke's historical usage.

why: εὖ occurs 6 times in the Byzantine (Majority) New Testament, across 5 books.

The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “well” in 3 of those places (50%), e.g. Luke 19:17; Acts 15:29. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 100% of the same verses.
The sense “well” is independently listed by Dodson, Strong's, the KJV glosses, corroborating the corpus evidence.
Attested secondary renderings: “Well done” (2×) — these mark the edges of its range, each verifiable at the citations given.
In the Septuagint it appears 40 times, most often translating the Hebrew יָטַב (H3190) (25×).
Moulton–Milligan documents this word in everyday papyri and inscriptions, anchoring the meaning in ordinary Koine usage outside the New Testament.
Moderate confidence: limited occurrences — the range shown is attested but may be incomplete.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'well' or 'rightly,' used as an exclamation of praise ('Well done!'), and in the phrase εὖ ποιεῖν meaning to help or do good.
prose.article: εὖ is a small adverb that mostly means "well" or "rightly" (used in 3 of its 6 New Testament occurrences), but it also serves as an exclamation of praise, "Well done!", as a master commends his servants in Matthew 25:21, 23. In the Septuagint it appears 40 times and usually renders the Hebrew yatav (25×), "to do well" or "to make good," often in set phrases like "to do good to" someone. Notably, Moulton-Milligan observe that εὖ became rare in everyday papyri, where καλῶς largely replaced it, though it lingered in polite letter-writing phrases like "please" and "farewell."
prose.caution: With only 6 occurrences, the line between the plain adverb "well," the exclamation "Well done!", and the phrase "do good to" depends on context, and Abbott-Smith notes some manuscripts read εὖγε or εὐποιεῖν instead.

issues: Sense label 3 'do good to' does not match the corpus-measured sense 'help whenever' (MAR 14:7); the label misrepresents the actual phrase εὖ ποιεῖν in context
The definition omits the 'help whenever / do good' sense entirely in its main wording, ignoring 17% of NT occurrences
LUK 19:17 is ambiguous: Abbott-Smith and Westcott-Hort read εὖγε there rather than εὖ, so listing it under 'Well done' without qualification may mislead readers about the textual situation

receipts.how: The master's reply 'Well done, good and faithful servant' is the clearest NT instance of εὖ as an exclamation of praise, confirming sense 2.
'That it may go well with you' uses εὖ as a plain adverb modifying the implied verb of faring, confirming sense 1.

'You can help them whenever you wish' renders εὖ ποιεῖν as a verb idiom meaning to do good/help, showing the definition's label 'do good to' is too narrow and that this sense is distinct from a bare adverb.

prose.def: Eve, the first woman and wife of Adam, mentioned in the New Testament as an example of deception and in a creation-order argument.
prose.article: Εὖα is simply the proper name Eve, the first woman, mentioned twice in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Timothy 2:13). The name comes from the Hebrew חַוָּה (Chavvah), introduced in Genesis 3:20. Both occurrences are rendered "Eve" unanimously, with no variation in meaning. One curious detail: in the Septuagint one of its two appearances corresponds not to חַוָּה but to הֶבֶל, suggesting a textual or transmission quirk in that passage.
prose.caution: This is a rare proper name with only two NT uses, and the Septuagint evidence shows an odd Hebrew correspondence worth noting.

issues: The definition omits Eve's role as wife of Adam, which is attested in Abbott-Smith and Dodson and is contextually relevant to both NT occurrences

The sense label is adequate but the definition could be tightened to match Dodson and Abbott-Smith by including the spousal relationship

receipts.how: Paul names Eve explicitly as the woman deceived by the serpent, confirming the proper-name referent and her identity as the first woman.

Eve is named alongside Adam in a creation-order argument, where her role as wife of Adam is implicit in the paired reference, supporting the need to mention the spousal relationship in the definition.

audit.author_note: Paul (2 Corinthians) uses Eve as a typological warning about deception, while the Pauline Pastoral (1 Timothy) uses her in a creation-order argument; both uses are proper-name references but serve distinct theological rhetorical purposes.

The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “preach gospel” in 13 of those places (24%), e.g. Luke 9:6; Acts 8:25. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 100% of the same verses.

prose.def: To announce good news; in the New Testament, usually to preach the Christian gospel of salvation, though occasionally used for other glad tidings.
prose.article: This verb means to announce good news, and in the New Testament it overwhelmingly carries the specific sense of preaching the Christian gospel of salvation. Its range is fairly tight: across 55 occurrences the renderings cluster around "preach the gospel" (13×, the single most common) and "good news" (9×), with all the other renderings being variations on proclaiming or hearing that message. A nice piece of background comes from the papyri: a document from around the reign of Trajan or Hadrian uses the rare active form for a slave arriving to announce a military victory, showing the word's everyday Koine use for spreading good tidings. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew בָּשַׂר ("to bring news," 18 of 22 times).

issues: Syntactic role data shows 49 of 55 occurrences tagged 'vocative', which is almost certainly a data anomaly or parsing label mismatch, yet the definition and article ignore this entirely and make no note of it

Sense 5 ('news') at 7% of occurrences includes 1TH 3:6 where Paul uses the verb for Timothy bringing ordinary personal news about the Thessalonians' faith and love — not strictly gospel proclamation — a non-evangelistic use the definition's 'especially' qualifier barely covers and the article glosses over

The definition is verb-infinitive form which is correct, but it does not acknowledge the middle/passive voice uses (Abbott-Smith explicitly notes passive uses: things 'proclaimed as glad tidings' and persons 'having glad tidings proclaimed to them'), which appear in the measured senses (e.g., sense 7, 8)
The article's claim that the word's range is 'fairly tight' understates the genuine active vs. middle/passive morphological variation that affects how readers parse subject and object in many verses
Dodson's note that the object can be 'expressed as a person' (e.g., proclaiming Jesus) is not reflected in the definition

receipts.how: Demonstrates the core sense: disciples go village to village preaching the gospel, directly supporting the definition's primary meaning.

Paul uses the verb for Timothy bringing personal news about the Thessalonians' faith and love, showing the word can extend beyond strict gospel proclamation and qualifying the definition's 'especially'.
Passive use ('the word...was preached to you') illustrates the middle/passive voice dimension the definition does not explicitly acknowledge.

audit.author_note: Paul (Galatians, Romans, 1–2 Corinthians) uses the verb with sharp theological focus on the content of the gospel message, while Luke (Luke, Acts) uses it more broadly for the act of announcing good news in narrative contexts, and 1TH 3:6 shows Paul himself using it once for non-gospel tidings, a nuance ordinary readers of those books should know.

prose.def: The good news of God's kingdom and salvation through Christ — the gospel message itself.
prose.article: In the New Testament εὐαγγέλιον means the good news — almost always the message of salvation through Christ — and it is rendered "gospel" in 73 of its 77 Byzantine occurrences (97%). The word often carries a defining genitive: it can name the giver (God), the subject (Christ, the kingdom), or the human messenger who delivers it. One striking piece of evidence is the Priene calendar inscription from about 9 B.C., which uses the plural to call the birthday of the Emperor Augustus the beginning of "tidings of joy" for the world — showing the word's wider Koine use for any momentous good announcement, while in classical Greek it could even mean a reward for bringing good news.

receipts.how: Mark opens his entire narrative as 'the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ,' demonstrating εὐαγγέλιον as the message of salvation through Christ — the core of the definition.
Matthew uses the genitive construction 'gospel of the kingdom,' confirming the definition's note that the word names its subject (God's kingdom) and remains rendered 'gospel' throughout.

Paul calls the gospel 'the power of God for salvation,' directly corroborating the definition's framing of εὐαγγέλιον as the message of salvation — and showing Paul's characteristic theological density with the term.

audit.author_note: Paul dominates usage (≈50 of 77 occurrences across his letters) and consistently frames εὐαγγέλιον in dense theological terms tied to justification and apostolic commission, whereas Mark uses it as a narrative heading and Matthew pairs it with 'the kingdom'; a reader moving between these authors will encounter the same word in subtly different rhetorical frames.

prose.def: A person who proclaims the gospel of Jesus Christ, recognized in the NT as a distinct ministry role alongside apostles and teachers.
senseLabels: evangelist as a ministry function or charge (2TI 4:5)
prose.article: An εὐαγγελιστής is someone who announces good news—in the New Testament specifically a preacher of the gospel. The word appears only 3 times across 3 books (Acts 21:8, Ephesians 4:11, 2 Timothy 4:5), and despite the varied surface renderings in the data, every instance points to the same role. It comes from εὐαγγελίζω ("to bring good news"), and one intriguing piece of evidence is a disputed inscription from Rhodes where the word may describe a chief priest as a "proclaimer" of oracular announcements—though scholars read that text differently. Abbott-Smith notes that only later, in church usage, did the word come to mean a writer of a gospel.
prose.caution: With just 3 occurrences and confidence rated low, the evidence is thin, and the cited Rhodes inscription is itself textually disputed.

classical.lsj: εὐαγγελ-ιστής , οῦ , ὁ , bringer of good tidings : hence, evangelist, preacher of the gospel, Act.Ap. 21.8 . proclaimer of oracular messages, IG 12(1).675 ( Rhodes ).

issues: Sense label 1 ('Leaving companions evangelist') is a garbled translation artifact, not a meaningful semantic label — it conflates narrative context with the word's meaning

The definition is substantively correct but does not distinguish the NT sense (gospel preacher) from the later ecclesiastical sense (gospel writer) mentioned by Abbott-Smith, which could confuse readers

The supporting article references the disputed Rhodes inscription, which Moulton-Milligan explicitly presents as uncertain and contested — introducing unnecessary doubt about a well-attested NT meaning
BSB independent agreement is 0% for ACT 21:8, the primary exemplar, which signals the sense label for that occurrence is unreliable and warrants flagging

receipts.how: Philip is called 'the evangelist,' demonstrating the NT sense of a traveling gospel preacher distinct from the apostles, confirming the core definition.
Evangelists are listed as a distinct gifted role alongside apostles, prophets, pastors, and teachers, supporting the definition of a recognized gospel-proclamation office.
Timothy is urged to 'do the work of an evangelist,' showing the term describes an active function of gospel proclamation, not merely a title, and where the definition holds cleanly.

audit.author_note: Luke (Acts) uses the term as a descriptive identifier for Philip in a narrative context, while Paul (Ephesians, 2 Timothy) uses it as a functional-ecclesiastical category and an imperative charge — readers of Acts encounter a biographical label whereas Pauline readers encounter a churchly office or duty.

prose.def: To be well-pleasing to someone (especially God), or in the passive, for someone to be well pleased with an action.
senseLabels: to be well-pleasing (active/middle) / to be well pleased (passive)
prose.article: In the New Testament this verb appears only 3 times, all in Hebrews, where it consistently means being well-pleasing—especially to God (Hebrews 11:5-6) or, in the passive, God being well pleased with our actions (Hebrews 13:16). The Septuagint uses it 13 times, notably for the Hebrew verb meaning 'to walk,' as in the descriptions of Enoch and Noah who 'walked with God' (Genesis 5:22, 24)—so the idea of pleasing God is tied to faithfully walking with him. Dodson suggests it can carry the added sense of rendering good service, and the word also shows up in everyday Koine, including a marriage contract from Egypt.

audit.author_note: All three NT occurrences are confined to Hebrews, so no cross-author variation can be measured; the definition's cultic and sacrificial nuance is specific to Hebrews' context.
